question: A 25-year-old with myopia of −4.00 D requests LASIK. Corneal topography reveals an inferior steepening pattern consistent with early keratoconus. What is the most appropriate course of action?

answers.text: Proceed with LASIK but ablate a smaller zone to preserve central corneal thickness

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This is dangerous. LASIK ablation further thins an already structurally weak cornea, risking post-LASIK ectasia — a devastating, irreversible complication.

answers.text: Decline LASIK and all corneal laser procedures; refer for corneal collagen cross-linking (CXL) assessment and consider phakic IOL if correction is needed

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Keratoconus is an absolute contraindication to all corneal laser refractive surgery. CXL can halt progression; if refractive correction is still needed, a phakic IOL avoids further corneal ablation.

answers.text: Perform PRK instead of LASIK, as PRK does not create a flap and is safer in keratoconus

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: PRK also ablates corneal stroma. Any surface laser ablation in keratoconus risks ectasia. PRK is not a safe alternative — the contraindication applies to all corneal laser procedures.

answers.text: Repeat topography in 6 months; proceed with LASIK if the pattern is stable

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Stability does not make keratoconus a safe indication for LASIK. Even stable early keratoconus is a contraindication because the post-ablation cornea may decompensate under normal intraocular pressure.

overallFeedback.feedback: Keratoconus is the most critical contraindication in refractive surgery. Any form of corneal ablation in a keratoconic eye risks post-operative ectasia. Always screen with topography before LASIK/PRK/SMILE.

Key principle: keratoconus = absolute contraindication to ALL corneal laser surgery. Screen every patient with topography before refractive surgery — post-LASIK ectasia is preventable only by pre-operative detection.
